title: The "cave of John the Baptist" near Suba
html:
The "cave of John the Baptist" near Suba

In 2004 the archaeologist Shimon Gibson published a cave on Kibbutz Tzuba, west of Jerusalem, proposing it as a place John used. The identification is the most contested item in this collection.

What is in the cave

A rock-cut installation with a plastered basin and channels, a carved standing figure holding a staff, and Iron Age and later pottery. Gibson's reading is that the basin and channels served a purification ritual, that the figure is a schematic holy man, and that Byzantine-era inscriptions and pilgrimage use show later veneration of the spot.

Why the identification is disputed

James F. Strange's review, in Biblical Archaeology Review, accepted the interest of the ritual installation while rejecting the chain of inference: an uninscribed figure cannot be identified as John, plastered basins of this kind are not unique, and later veneration would demonstrate only that later communities believed something about the cave — not what happened in it in the first century. The gaps between "ritual installation", "figure", "John" and "this cave" are each filled by argument, not by finds.

The monograph remains useful as a report on the installation. It is not evidence that John lived in, taught in, or baptized anyone in that cave.

Read more

  • James F. Strange, review of The Cave of John the Baptist, Biblical Archaeology Review, 2011.
